title: What Are Fossils?
description: How ancient life is preserved in rock — and why most of it isn't

concepts.title: Defining Fossils
concepts.contentHtml:
A fossil is any evidence of past life preserved in rock. Most people think of bones or shells, but fossils include:

  • Body fossils — actual remains (bones, shells, teeth, wood).
  • Trace fossils — evidence of behaviour (footprints, burrows, bite marks, coprolites/fossilised droppings).
  • Chemical fossils — organic molecules preserved in rock, including the oldest evidence of life (~3.5 billion years ago).

Fossilisation is exceedingly rare. Soft tissue almost never survives; hard mineralised parts (shells, bones) are far more likely to be preserved. The fossil record is a tiny, biased sample of past life.

concepts.title: How Fossilisation Happens
concepts.contentHtml:
For a fossil to form, an organism must be buried rapidly in sediment before it decomposes. The most common process is permineralisation: minerals dissolved in groundwater gradually replace organic material or fill pore spaces, turning soft tissue to stone while preserving structure.

Other preservation modes:
— Amber — organisms trapped in tree resin that hardens; preserves insects with exquisite detail.
— Tar pits (e.g. La Brea, Los Angeles) — animals mired in asphalt, preserving bones.
— Permafrost — entire woolly mammoths preserved frozen for tens of thousands of years.
— Compression — thin carbon film left after burial and pressure (plant fossils).

concepts.title: The Bias of the Fossil Record
concepts.contentHtml:
The fossil record is not a random sample of past life. Several biases affect what is preserved:

  • Preservation bias — hard parts survive; soft-bodied organisms are under-represented.
  • Habitat bias — marine environments deposit sediment; forests rarely do.
  • Abundance bias — common organisms are more likely to be fossilised than rare ones.
  • Discovery bias — fossils only found where rocks are exposed, excavated, and searched.

Despite these limitations, the fossil record is an extraordinary archive. Paleontologists use statistical methods to correct for sampling biases and reconstruct past biodiversity from incomplete data.

title: The History of Life
description: From single cells to complex ecosystems across 4 billion years

concepts.title: The Precambrian — Life's Long Dawn
concepts.contentHtml:
Life originated approximately 3.7–3.5 billion years ago — chemical fossils and stromatolites (layered mats of cyanobacteria) are the oldest evidence. For most of Earth's history, life was entirely microbial.

Around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria evolved oxygenic photosynthesis and began flooding the atmosphere with O₂ — the Great Oxidation Event. This was catastrophic for anaerobic life but eventually made complex aerobic life possible.

The first multicellular animals appear in the Ediacaran period (~635–541 Ma): soft-bodied, enigmatic organisms like Dickinsonia that are difficult to classify into any modern group.

concepts.title: The Cambrian Explosion
concepts.contentHtml:
At the start of the Cambrian period (~541 Ma), nearly all major animal body plans (phyla) appear in the fossil record within a geologically short interval of ~20–25 million years — the Cambrian Explosion.

The Burgess Shale of British Columbia (505 Ma) preserves an extraordinary window into this world: soft-bodied animals including Anomalocaris (a top predator), Opabinia (five eyes, a flexible nozzle), and the earliest chordates. Discovered by Charles Walcott in 1909, it remains the most important Cambrian fossil site.

The explosion may have been triggered by rising oxygen levels, ecological arms races, or environmental change — the cause is still debated.

concepts.title: Paleozoic Life — Colonising Land
concepts.contentHtml:
During the Paleozoic era (541–252 Ma), life colonised land. The key transitions:

  • Ordovician–Silurian: first vascular land plants (~430 Ma).
  • Devonian: forests of tree-sized plants; first tetrapods (four-limbed vertebrates) emerge from the sea. Tiktaalik (~375 Ma) is a famous transitional fossil: a fish with limb-like fins and a neck.
  • Carboniferous: coal swamp forests; amphibians dominate; first reptiles evolve from tetrapods.
  • Permian: reptiles diversify; mammal-like reptiles (synapsids) become the dominant land vertebrates — until the P-T extinction (~252 Ma) nearly erased them.

title: Mass Extinctions
description: The five great die-offs and what caused them

concepts.title: The Big Five Mass Extinctions
concepts.contentHtml:
The fossil record reveals five major mass extinctions — events where global biodiversity dropped by >50 % in a geologically short time:

  1. Ordovician–Silurian (~443 Ma) — glaciation and sea-level fall; ~85 % of marine species lost.
  2. Late Devonian (~375 Ma) — ~75 % species loss; cause unclear.
  3. Permian–Triassic (~252 Ma) — the 'Great Dying'; ~96 % of marine species, ~70 % of terrestrial species.
  4. Triassic–Jurassic (~201 Ma) — ~80 % species loss; opened ecological space for dinosaurs.
  5. Cretaceous–Paleogene (~66 Ma) — ~76 % of species; ended non-avian dinosaurs.

concepts.title: The Permian–Triassic: The Great Dying
concepts.contentHtml:
The Permian–Triassic (P-T) extinction ~252 million years ago was the most severe in Earth's history — sometimes called the 'Great Dying'. It nearly ended complex life on Earth.

The primary cause is believed to be the Siberian Traps LIP: massive volcanic eruptions over ~2 million years releasing CO₂, SO₂, and methane into the atmosphere, causing rapid warming, ocean acidification, and anoxia (oxygen depletion in seawater).

Recovery took ~10 million years. The survivors included the archosaurs, which would eventually give rise to dinosaurs and crocodiles, and a small number of mammal-like reptiles, which would eventually give rise to mammals.

concepts.title: The K-Pg Extinction and the Chicxulub Impact
concepts.contentHtml:
The most famous extinction — the end of the non-avian dinosaurs — occurred 66 million years ago at the K-Pg boundary, caused by the impact of an ~10 km diameter asteroid at Chicxulub, on the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico.

The impact released energy equivalent to billions of nuclear bombs, triggering wildfires, a 'nuclear winter' from dust blocking sunlight, and ocean acidification. About 76 % of all species were lost.

Survivors included birds (avian dinosaurs), small mammals, turtles, and crocodilians. The extinction cleared ecological space that mammals then diversified to fill — leading eventually to primates, and to humans.

title: Famous Fossil Sites
description: The quarries and cliffs that rewrote the history of life

concepts.title: Burgess Shale — Window on the Cambrian
concepts.contentHtml:
The Burgess Shale in the Canadian Rockies of British Columbia was discovered by Charles Walcott in 1909. It preserves the soft-bodied animals of a Cambrian marine community (~505 Ma) in extraordinary detail — creatures that would normally leave no trace.

Among its famous taxa:
— Anomalocaris: up to 1 m long, the apex predator of its day.
— Hallucigenia: a bizarre worm-like creature with spines and tentacles.
— Pikaia: a possible early chordate — perhaps a distant ancestor of vertebrates.

The Burgess Shale transformed understanding of the Cambrian Explosion by showing the full diversity of animal life from which all modern phyla descended.

concepts.title: La Brea Tar Pits — Ice Age Megafauna
concepts.contentHtml:
The La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles, California are one of the world's richest Ice Age fossil sites. Natural petroleum seeps to the surface, forming sticky asphalt pools that trapped animals over the past ~50,000 years.

The pits have yielded over 3.5 million fossils including:
— Saber-toothed cats (Smilodon fatalis)
— Dire wolves (Aenocyon dirus)
— Columbian mammoths and mastodons
— Giant ground sloths and short-faced bears

The La Brea fauna disappeared in the end-Pleistocene megafauna extinction (~12,000 years ago), coinciding with both climate change and the arrival of humans in North America.

concepts.title: Solnhofen and Messel — Exceptional Preservation
concepts.contentHtml:
Some fossil sites preserve life in near-perfect detail, earning the German term Lagerstätten ('storage places').

Solnhofen Limestone, Germany (~150 Ma, Late Jurassic): fine-grained limestone quarried for printing stone. It famously preserves Archaeopteryx — the first bird — with feather impressions. Thirteen specimens are known, and each new discovery refines our understanding of the dinosaur-to-bird transition.

Messel Pit, Germany (~47 Ma, Eocene): a former maar lake. It preserves early horses the size of foxes, bats with gut contents, and insects with original colour pigments. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most scientifically productive fossil sites in the world.

title: Frontiers in Paleontology
description: Ancient DNA, feathered dinosaurs, and the sixth extinction

concepts.title: Feathered Dinosaurs and the Bird Transition
concepts.contentHtml:
The discovery of feathered dinosaurs in Cretaceous deposits of Liaoning, China since the 1990s has provided overwhelming evidence that birds are living avian dinosaurs — a direct evolutionary continuation of theropod dinosaurs, not merely their descendants.

Key fossils include Sinosauropteryx (first non-avian dinosaur found with feather impressions, 1996), Microraptor (four-winged glider), and dozens of others. Combined with Archaeopteryx from Solnhofen, these specimens trace the gradual acquisition of feathers, wishbones, and flight adaptations step by step.

The implication: dinosaurs are not extinct. About 10,000 species of avian dinosaurs (birds) are alive today.

concepts.title: Ancient DNA and Palaeogenomics
concepts.contentHtml:
The sequencing of ancient DNA (aDNA) from preserved specimens has revolutionised understanding of recent evolution. Key findings:

  • Neanderthal genome (2010, Svante Pääbo's team): modern non-African humans carry ~2 % Neanderthal DNA, confirming interbreeding.
  • Denisovans — an entirely new hominin species identified from a single finger bone in Siberia, known only from its genome.
  • Woolly mammoth — nearly complete genome; discussions of 'de-extinction' using gene editing.

DNA degrades over time and rarely survives beyond ~1 million years even in permafrost. The study of ancient proteins (palaeoproteomics) can reach further back — horse proteins have been sequenced from ~1.7 million year old dental enamel.

concepts.title: The Sixth Extinction
concepts.contentHtml:
Paleontologists have used the fossil record to estimate background extinction rates — the natural rate at which species disappear between mass extinctions. Current extinction rates are estimated at 100–1,000 times the background rate, driven by habitat destruction, climate change, invasive species, and overexploitation.

Biologist E.O. Wilson argued we are in the early stages of a sixth mass extinction. The Pleistocene megafauna collapse (~50,000–10,000 years ago) — when most large land mammals outside Africa disappeared, correlating with human expansion — may mark its beginning.

The fossil record teaches us that mass extinctions are survivable by life as a whole, but recoveries take millions of years. What is lost cannot be recovered on human timescales.
